title: Equities: Middle East, RBA set tone ahead of earnings rush
full_text:
The stalemate in the Middle East conflict and growing expectations for another Reserve Bank interest rate rise set a bearish tone for the Australian sharemarket ahead of one of the busiest weeks of the year for local corporate earnings reports.
S&P/ASX 200 Index futures point to a 0.4 per cent drop at Monday's open, extending last week's losses after more companies missed profit expectations than beat them last week.
Traders are bracing for the trend to continue, with bourse heavyweights including BHP, CSL, and National Australia Bank all set to report next week.
Emanuel Datt, chief investment officer at Datt Capital, said that while the local sharemarket overall maintained an "upward bias" which pushed it to record highs less than a fortnight ago, earnings season was dividing the market.
Stocks with exposure to downtrodden consumers or the soft real estate market were particularly at risk, he added.
"Retail names seem to be downgrading [forward earnings] guidance or softening their language around guidance," he said, citing Treasury Wine Estates and Endeavour Group as examples. Both alcoholic beverage companies have posted large profit drops in recent weeks, with investors set to get a peak under the hood this week at other listed retailers including JB Hi-Fi and Super Retail Group.
Tuesday will also bring the latest Westpac/Melbourne Institute consumer sentiment index, which the bank's economists said could show the housing market downturn and expiry of the fuel excise discount weighing on households.
Beyond individual company results, the RBA's next moves are also weighing on market sentiment. While the central bank held rates as expected last Tuesday, governor Michele Bullock's hawkish press conference stoked concerns that a fourth increase in borrowing costs remained firmly on the cards this year, even as the housing market downturn deepens across the country.
"We've already raised three times, and we will go again if we need to, and I think personally that it's quite possible we might need to go [again]. But we'll wait and see what the data tells us," Bullock said on Tuesday, adding that a rate cut was not even considered by the monetary policy board.
That speculation will only intensify this week if wages or labour data releases due on Wednesday and Thursday morning respectively come in hotter than expected, or if RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser doubles down on Bullock's comments when he speaks in Brisbane on Wednesday afternoon.
Labour data - which is especially closely watched by traders as a pointer to the RBA's future rate calls -is expected to show the unemployment rate steady at 4.4 per cent, and a big drop in employment gains from 76,300 people finding work in June to just 11,400 in July.
The nearly six-month-old war in the Middle East - which investors have largely learned to live with - could also force the RBA's hand if it takes another turn for the worse and pushes up the oil price.
Datt said that if the crude oil price rose to above $US90 ($127) and stayed there for at least a month, "that would be like waving a red flag to a bull for the RBA".
"They have to be proactive about controlling or mitigating inflation, and [an interest rate increase] is their single biggest lever to do that," he added.
Global benchmark Brent crude traded just below $US89 on Sunday, having fluctuated in a narrow range between $US85 and $US90 for the last few weeks.
Iran and Oman are gradually progressing towards a deal to open a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, while Tehran's negotiations with the United States have stalled.
"For now, oil seems to have become the proverbial dog that barks loudly but ultimately never bites," a team of analysts led by Barclays' head of economics research Christian Keller told clients on Sunday AEST.
"We do not claim that this will change soon, but given the surprising calm in recent weeks, the risk seems tilted for potentially more pressure in the coming weeks."
The dip in ASX futures markets followed narrow move downs on all three Wall Street indices on Friday (Saturday AEST), as weak United States retail sales data hurt investor sentiment - the latest in a series of inflation, employment and spending statistics which suggest the world's largest economy is cooling.
